title: Operator Tax & Deployment Risk — Sales/Messaging Brief
content:
Purpose:
Quick reference for sales and PMs to qualify prospects who are evaluating building on vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM vs buying Redwood. Focus is operator surface, risk vectors, and tight messaging hooks that resonate with platform/infra buyers.

Audience:
- Platform engineers and infra leads at mid-market and enterprise product orgs
- CTO/VP Eng for smaller orgs that still own their inference stack

Core thesis (one-liner):
Most teams underestimate the ongoing operational tax of self-hosted inference — not just raw $/token, but upgrade friction, kernel and quantization maintenance, capacity variance, and product feature parity (streaming, evals, rollouts). Redwood converts those recurring risks into predictable SLAs, tooling, and migration lanes.

Key operator risk buckets (how to frame):
1) Upgrade and compatibility tax
- Drivers: CUDA, cuBLAS/cuDNN, Triton bindings, Python wheels, kernel regressions.
- Impact: weekly/biweekly break-fix windows during infra upgrades; emergent hotfixes after driver/model changes.
- Messaging hook: "We absorb kernel and driver churn so your SREs don't have to babysit every model release."

2) Performance regression & model-variant management
- Drivers: tuning for quantized kernels, attention-kernel mismatches, KV-cache edge cases at scale.
- Impact: silent P99 latency regressions and throughput drops that only show up under production traffic.
- Messaging hook: "Pin models + rollback policies + verified performance baselines — reduce surprise regressions during releases."

3) Cost drift and capacity forecasting
- Drivers: variable token mix, tail-latency-driven overprovisioning, GPU fragmentation (holes in utilization).
- Impact: teams overcommit reserved GPUs or continually pay for burst capacity they can’t use efficiently.
- Messaging hook: "Reduce capex-like reserved capacity and get predictable unit economics with autoscaling and burst lanes."

4) Feature parity & product risk
- Drivers: streaming, function/tool calling, structured outputs, eval hooks, hybrid routing.
- Impact: product teams lose velocity because self-hosted components lag on features customers expect.
- Messaging hook: "Same API/SDK and runtime features across hosted/dedicated/private — no rework when you scale."

5) Security, compliance, and audit burden
- Drivers: KMS/HSM integrations, private VPCs, SOC/PCI patterns for logs and egress.
- Impact: heavy engineering lift for audit-readiness and maintaining certs.
- Messaging hook: "We provide enterprise-grade private deployments and audit-traceability so your security team can sign off faster."

Operator Effort Scorecard (simple qualifier to use in discovery):
- Initial setup time (estimate): prototype: 4–8 weeks; production hardening: 3–6 months
- Core team required: 1 infra/ML infra eng + 1 ML engineer for model compatibility + SRE on-call coverage
- Ongoing cadence: monthly upgrades, continuous kernel tuning, per-release QA for major models
- Estimated ops FTE equivalent after year 1: 0.5–2.0 FTEs for mid-market workloads; 2–6 FTEs for high-throughput enterprise (qualitative guidance).

Common buyer rationales (and counters):
- "We already use vLLM/TGI locally, it's cheap."
  Counter: total cost = infra + ops + downtime/bugs. We provide unit economics analyses including token-level breakdowns and hidden ops tax.
- "We need full control due to compliance."
  Counter: Redwood Private offers VPC/on-prem lifecycle + KMS integrations; transfer control without rebuilding orchestration and SLO tooling.
- "We can hire the engineers."
  Counter: hiring hides risk: recruiting time, ramp, tribal knowledge. For many teams we calculate a 6–12 month TCO breakeven in transactional workloads.

Sales qualification checklist (questions to ask):
- What is your current 95/99th percentile latency SLO for LLM endpoints?
- How often do you upgrade CUDA/driver stacks or add new model families per quarter?
- Who owns token-level cost attribution and how accurate are current numbers?
- Have you had production regressions after model changes? Frequency?
- What security/audit controls are mandatory for sign-off (VPC, KMS, SOC2, etc)?

Objection handling snippets (short):
- "We can tune vLLM ourselves" -> "You can — but it's a continuous tax. We do this at scale and can show before/after unit economics for your workload in an eval."
- "Managed will be more expensive" -> "Compare TCO: include SRE/ML-ramp, outages, and lost velocity. Our Optimize tooling often reduces per-token cost via batching/caching and quantization guidance to offset fees."

Suggested lead-gen hooks and content pieces (3 prioritized):
1) "Ops Tax Calculator" — a short interactive worksheet estimating FTEs, upgrade windows, and hidden monthly costs for self-hosted inference. Use as qualification landing asset.
2) "Kernel & Upgrade War Stories" — a 1–2 page narrative with anonymized incidents (regressions after driver updates, cold-start KV cache bugs) to humanize risks.
3) "Migration lane playbook" — step-by-step migration lanes: quick POC (hosted), staging on Dedicated, lift to Private (if needed).

Playbook snippet: 30–60 day migration lane (sales-assisted POC)
- Day 0–7: onboarding, ingest 1–2 sample prompts, baseline latency/cost on their model(s)
- Day 7–21: enable caching/batching suggestions from Redwood Optimize, measure delta
- Day 21–45: run canary traffic, validate fallback policies and rollouts, generate TCO comparison
- Day 45–60: handoff to infra with runbook and optional Dedicated contract

Metrics to show during POC (priority order):
- P99 latency and P50 latency delta vs current stack
- Cost per 1k tokens (including inferred infra/ops)
- Time-to-first-fix for a simulated kernel regression
- Number of manual upgrade hours avoided/month

Sample outreach email (short):
"Quick question — curious how your team budgets for inference upgrades. Many infra teams we talk to are surprised by the recurring ops time after an initial vLLM/TGI rollout. We built a 10-minute Ops Tax Calculator that maps your monthly upgrade hours to a TCO number — would you like the link?"

Open items / research asks (internal):
- Collect 3 anonymized incident stories with rough MTTD/MTTR numbers to make Kernel War Stories concrete.
- Quantify a few workload archetypes (chatty chat, long-form generation, embedding-heavy) with estimate FTE numbers and expected GPU types.
- Capture recent compatibility issues between TGI/vLLM and Triton/TF kernels to add to risk appendix.

One-paragraph positioning blurb for battlecards:
"Redwood reduces the invisible tax of running inference: we handle kernel upgrades, performance tuning, and capacity economics so your engineers can ship product features instead of endless infra triage. For teams that need ultimate control, our Private deployments give the audit controls they need without rebuilding the orchestration and SLO tooling from scratch."

Next steps for GTM:
- Share this doc with AE enablement + draft Ops Tax Calculator prototype (owner: Jenna Liu)
- Create an internal 1-pager for SDRs with top 3 qualification questions and the quick outreach email (owner: Miguel Santos)
- Pull anonymized incident examples from applied-ml and serving-runtime teams (owner: Omar Rahman)

Notes to self: keep the tone concrete and operator-focused — avoid abstract cost-per-token comparisons only. Ops stories and concrete time-savings close deals.
